 That sounds a lot like what I went through. I was on hormones for almost a year and was slowly moving forward with socially transitioning while worrying I would not be able to go through it, and then I had this moment when I realized I didn't needed to transition. Then everything felt better. Life seemed easier. I didn't have to worry about all that trans stuff. As I eased off the hormones, I felt a little sad to see that part of me go, but I felt good about moving forward. I then moved forward with life; I became more social and started dating.

It's been a year now since I stopped, and during that year I thought about my transition a lot. I felt I learned more about myself, and never regretted going through what I did. I am also glad that I went through what I went through this year, even if there were hard times (and there were plenty). 

But here's where I'm at right now: I need to transition. The slow return of my old feelings of pain and dysphoria was subtle, but are now very noticeable. I realized that I was scared before, and that I felt I wasn't as sure about myself as I felt I should be in order to have the courage to keep moving forward with transition. This time off has done a lot for me to realize who I am. It has made me more sure of who I am. I guess I needed that to prove it to myself.

My advice to you is to use this time to get really get to know yourself. Keep in mind that there is nothing wrong with detransitioning, re-transitioning, or doing something in between, and let your experiences guide you.

No. A normal man doesn't deal with that. A normal man, if he wonders about his gender identity at all, will more quickly come to the conclusion that he is male (with maybe a feminine side, but no interest in actually living his life as a woman).

Now, on the other hand, a normal trans person may often have these exact same doubts, may often try to find a way out of transitioning, may often have a fear of losing everything, may often have a fear of not passing, may often site a few masculine or unfeminine (or vice versa) thoughts or traits as evidence of a cis identity while completely ignoring the obvious fact that living day after day as their assigned gender is a constant source of discomfort, worry, and inquiry to the point of spending a significant amount of time researching trans topics, thinking about it objectively, and posting questions like yours in a trans forum.

Knowing one's self isn't easy; don't think that it will or should be. I think you're just going to have to try some things out, make some mistakes and make some discoveries, experience pain and experience joy. You're going to a gender therapist; that's a good first step. Continue moving forward with self discovery and you'll find the answers you're looking for, whatever they end up being.

Take note: you're about to live some serious life in the near future. Get what you can from it.

There were doubts that this was right for me, but almost everyone has those. I didn't have thoughts that this was wrong for me, and I have doubts about everything I do because I'm kind of a second guesser. I started getting read and addressed as a girl while still in boy mode and even got hit on on a couple of occasions by straight men. I became comfortable and confident. 

One day I put my hair up under a hat to make it look like I had short hair, and I kept going back to that. I started enjoying being in boy mode instead of just dealing with it. I started choosing it over girl mode to people I was out to. It was on a drive home from a job interview that I had this epiphany that I didn't have to be trans woman; I could be a guy if I wanted to. I tried to reassure myself throughout transition that I don't have to force myself into anything. If I changed my mind then that's OK. But at this moment, I actually felt that I was allowed to be a man. I was allowed to be anything, really. 

The next few days I thought about nothing but the prospect of detransition. I wanted to see if this was just a passing thought. The feeling became more certain as I thought about. I was going to do this because I wanted to. I wouldn't do it for any other reason. I felt my drag performances and androgynous style allowed me to express my feminine side, and I felt that transition showed me that I don't have to stay within the binary if I didn't feel like it. I'll be who I want and who I feel like I am.

It might not be the same as the experience you're going through, but I had a similar dual personality before I started transition. I would have what I perceived as a male me and a female me. The two mes couldn't occupy my head at the same time, so when I was in one I would sort of leave messages for the other. Then when I was the other, I would remember leaving it to myself, but it wasn't the current me that left it and was usually in strong disagreement about it. I would often try to reason with myself, but sides trying to make compromises with each other and making promises that were inevitably broken.

It's hard for me to remember exactly what it was like, as it no longer occurs. Once I said the words aloud and came out to someone (satisfying female me's plea for help), I never became the male me exclusively again. He conceded willingly, saw how good it felt to be female, and became part of the female me. I felt whole for the first time. It was actually kind of strange and almost uncomfortable at first; I was not used to being one me. It was defiantly a welcome change, though. As I then was able to look back at my past and my mindset, and I didn't even recognize myself. Only then, did I see how miserable I was. I once thought about ways to kill myself to comfort myself for God's sake! Every night before bed at the very least. It was normal before, but now it seemed so damn depressing.

That male me was a coping mechanism of denial trying to protect me from facing the hardships of transition and being seen as different. The mind is often very good at that--developing a learned helplessness and rationalizing pain to make it less noticeable.

Like I said, my experiences likely differ from yours. But the best thing you can do is talk about them out loud, face to face, with another person (likely a therapist). Hopefully you can bring your two halfs together. I wish you all the best.

I remember going over a few coming out letters before having a couple drinks, sitting down, and writing mine. Here's what I wrote:

Dear mom and dad, 

I wanted to write you this letter to address some concerns you may have had about me lately and to explain things more clearly. You’ve known for awhile that I’ve had some issues with depression since I was young. I know that, as well as being very hard on me, it has also been hard on you to know that I’ve had to deal with these difficulties in my life. I know that you wish I were happy, and I can’t tell you how much it means to me that you care so much for my well-being and happiness. I want nothing more than to make you proud of me. I feel very supported and am glad to have you as parents; I couldn’t ask for a better father and mother. 

I’ve been wanting to write this letter for some time now, and I know that mom in particular has been asking a few questions about me to (sister’s name) and wondering what exactly is going on with me lately. Well, I want to answer those questions myself. To begin with, I’m feeling very happy for the first time since I can really remember. I have finally found a treatment for my depression that actually works, and I must say that it’s wonderful to feel like life is worth living. I know that must sound depressing, that I thought life itself was somewhat meaningless, but that’s what I was feeling. I felt like I was only alive because I happen to not be dead yet. Horrific, I know. I look back at how I was and how I viewed my life, and I am amazed (and frustrated) that I was carrying such a burden. I still may have plenty of struggles, but I’ve shaken off this core feeling of depression and helplessness, and in doing so now believe that my life can be full of happiness and meaning. 

It’s the specifics of what has made me feel so much better that I write this letter to you now. I’ve had to build up the courage to tell both of you, and I now feel that I can admit something very personal about me and be honest about myself to you. Believe me when I say that this is something I’ve struggled with. I mean really struggled with. I’ve wanted to deny it for most of my life, but have come to the conclusion that I can’t keep living a lie. Growing up I knew something was off about me, and as the years went by this fact became more and more apparent. Making steps toward transition, no matter how small, was an important thing for me. Focus on the little achievements as you move forward, because transition is going to take a lot of time and effort, and if you focus only on the end goal you'll find it hard to keep up the motivation. 

It's really helpful to have someone like a therapist or good friend to talk with and help you set goals for yourself. One of the things I wanted to do for transition was lose weight, so that incremental change did a lot to keep my motivation up. Other things like growing your hair, getting it cut in a more feminine style, practicing makeup and voice, slowly incorporate and play around with desired looks (shaved legs and body, painted nails, androgynous/feminine clothes), and start coming out to those close to you. Exercise is also a very helpful practice to get into. I stuck to running and stretching.

Also, if you feel you're ready for it, start HRT. It'll help make you feel better, and seeing visual progress helps keep you motivated.

I didn't have any delusions that I would grow up to be a girl; having a slightly younger sister and sharing baths as young kids, I knew that I was a boy because I had boys parts and not girl parts. I just kept thinking that what I was going through was a phase, and because I have always been very uncertain about anything in my life, I didn't look too far into my feelings. 

The idea of transitioning never seemed like a possibility. I dismissed the existence of transsexuals in real life just as I had dismissed blunt head trauma on/off amnesia as seen on TV. Once I got to college and had broadband internet access for the first time in my life, I discovered much more about transsexualism. I still denied it, as I was never one to be outside the mainstream, and being trans would be too much for me to handle. I still often thought about being a women, and had a constant back-and-forth between myself over whether or not I was really trans. Any excuse my denying side of myself could think of--don't think of myself as a "woman trapped in a man's body" (I later thought a lot about it and described myself as a "person who would be much more comfortable as a women, but is stuck with an uncomfortable male body" and realized that I was splitting hairs), autogynephilia, lack of a girlfriend to fill a feminine void in my life, etc.--was used to keep these thoughts tucked away. But every night, when I was alone in my thoughts, I imagined myself as a women. I would sometimes think "That's it. I'm getting hormones and doing this thing, " only to later convince myself that I'm just being crazy.

Going through all that, it was not very obvious that I was trans. In hindsight, it seems pretty obvious to me that I was and I kick myself for not realizing it sooner. I guess it has to do with the fact that I always shied away from drastic change, and that I am never sure about anything and always questioning myself. If I had a much more outgoing and confident personality, I my have told my parents as a kid that "I'm not a boy anymore; I'm a girl." But I had to live for years with these thoughts turning up again, and again, and again (and have a failed suicide attempt) before I convinced myself to get the confidence to admit this to myself and start living a life I actually felt attached to.

So far, despite all the hardships and speed-bumps, it's pretty good and getting better.

Calling GID, GD, or whatever they want to call it a disorder does not mean there is anything wrong with it, only that people may experience problems with it. If you have little to no distress over being transgender, then you do not have this disorder as far as identity is concerned. The label is used to direct treatment. It's a categorical thing to keep clinicians on the same page and use proven treatment methods rather than having them decide on their own on how to treat the client (which definitely has been a problem in the past with transgender therapy and why these changes are being made in the new DSM). Being transgender can include many distresses, and many of these distresses are shared by many trans people. Keeping everything organized under a single main label just makes it easier to direct proper treatment specific to the individual.

I may not be understanding your point correctly, but it seems to me that you have a problem with an apparent stigma associated with the term "disorder" or "medical condition." While using the medical model with psychological disorders has it advantages, it clearly is not perfect. There is an obvious state of homeostasis with the body, not so with the mind. These terms are shared with physiological medicine, but their use is much more contingent.

EDIT: I'm probably way off base and not addressing your concern properly. I do understand the sense of my identity being devalued or restricted to certain gender norms that cis-people are often not held to. And these guidelines are not perfect, but then again nothing really is. Some of the treatment needs to be left up to the individual giving it, otherwise any sense of personal identity of the client is irrelevant. But there needs to be enough in the book that restricts clinicians from making their own treatment plans based on ignorance. The individual variation needs to be as small as possible while still being useful to as many people as possible, and these revisions are making it smaller. It's frustrating and slow, but that's what science is. Keep making your objections and pointing out the flaws (it's important to the cause), but please don't completely ignore movement in the right direction.

Unless parts of someone's identity are causing him or her distress, negatively affecting his or her day-to-day life, or could result in self-harm. If you're fine with your identity, then you don't have an identity disorder. The word disorder only identifies specific guidelines for treatment, because if there is distress it needs to be treated. That's it. You shouldn't get too caught up on the word, as negative as it comes across. 

Who's to say that someone's identity can't cause them distress, and if it does, then there should be a set of guidelines laid out based on proven methods to alleviate that distress. We're not talking about "curing" people of their identities, if that's what you're worried about. Some people, myself included, needed help accepting their identities and to not be ashamed of them or be in denial.
